facts.largest_city: Huntsville (215,006 people in the 2020 Census, passing Birmingham)
facts.nickname: Alabama has no official nickname; it is often called the Yellowhammer State, the Heart of Dixie, or the Cotton State.
facts.motto: Audemus jura nostra defendere (We Dare Maintain Our Rights)
facts.name_origin: Named for the Alabama people, an Indigenous nation that lived in western Alabama and eastern Mississippi until the early 1800s.

government.chambers: Alabama Senate (35 senators) and Alabama House of Representatives (105 representatives); all members serve four-year terms.
government.executive: Governor (elected every four years; may serve at most two terms in a row). The governor signs or vetoes bills, prepares the yearly state budget, appoints many department heads, and commands the state's military forces.
government.courts: Supreme Court of Alabama (9 justices: a chief justice and 8 associate justices; Alabama judges serve six-year terms); Court of Civil Appeals and Court of Criminal Appeals; 41 circuit courts; district courts in all 67 counties; 68 probate courts and 274 municipal courts.
government.local: 67 counties, each with a district court; cities and towns run municipal courts and local services.
government.constitution: Alabama's current constitution is the Constitution of 2022. Voters approved it on November 8, 2022 (76.49% yes). It reorganized the 1901 constitution and removed racist language, such as the ban on interracial marriage and the school segregation requirement. Article I, Section 32 now says: "That no form of slavery shall exist in this state; and there shall not be any involuntary servitude."
government.kid_line: "That all political power is inherent in the people, and all free governments are founded on their authority, and instituted for their benefit" (Alabama Constitution of 2022, Article I, Section 2).

long_ago.about: Around 1120, people built a planned town of 29 earthen mounds around a central plaza on the Black Warrior River. About 1,000 people lived inside its walls; they hunted, fished, and grew crops, especially corn.

The Creeks lived in east-central Alabama in a confederacy of 30 to 60 towns (talwa) along the Chattahoochee, Tallapoosa, and Coosa rivers. They grew corn, hunted deer, and held a midsummer busk (poskita) ceremony of four to eight days.
Choctaw towns stood along today's Alabama and Mississippi border near the Tombigbee River. Some scholars link their ancestors to the Moundville chiefdom.
The Cherokee Nation's land reached into northeast Alabama; about 1,200 Cherokees lived in Alabama before removal in 1838.
The state is named for this nation, which lived in western Alabama and eastern Mississippi until the early 1800s.

today.about: Alabama's only federally recognized tribe (recognized August 11, 1984). Its reservation is at Poarch, about eight miles from Atmore in Escambia County, and its ancestors are Creeks who stayed in Alabama.
A state-recognized tribe in Mobile and Washington counties in southwest Alabama.
One of nine tribes recognized by the Alabama Indian Affairs Commission.

today.nation: Ma-Chis Lower Creek Indian Tribe of Alabama
today.about: One of nine tribes recognized by the Alabama Indian Affairs Commission.

first_peoples.today_note: The Alabama Indian Affairs Commission (created by the legislature in 1984) lists nine state-recognized tribes: the Poarch Band of Creek Indians, Echota Cherokee Tribe of Alabama, Cherokee Tribe of Northeast Alabama, Ma-Chis Lower Creek Indian Tribe of Alabama, Star Clan of Muscogee Creeks, Cher-O-Creek Intra Tribal Indians, MOWA Band of Choctaw Indians, Piqua Shawnee Tribe, and United Cherokee Ani-Yun-Wiya Nation. Only the Poarch Band is federally recognized. Most Creek, Choctaw, and Cherokee people were forced west to Indian Territory (today's Oklahoma) in the 1830s.
sites: Moundville Archaeological Park, 14 miles south of Tuscaloosa (Mississippian mound town)
Horseshoe Bend National Military Park (site of the 1814 battle that ended the Creek War)
Fort Payne area, DeKalb County, where Alabama Cherokees camped before removal in 1838

history.event: Mississippian people settle Moundville on the Black Warrior River; it becomes a planned town of 29 mounds that lasts more than three centuries.
Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto's army enters Alabama. On October 18, 1540, at Mabila, the town of Chief Tascaluza, the Spanish set fire to the town and kill many people.
The French build Fort Louis de La Louisiane; the colony moves to present-day Mobile in 1711.
Spanish forces under Bernardo de Gálvez defeat the British at Fort Charlotte in Mobile during the American Revolution.
On March 27, Andrew Jackson's army, with Cherokee and Creek allies, defeats the Red Stick Creeks at Horseshoe Bend. The Creeks are forced to give up about 23 million acres.
On March 3, Congress creates the Alabama Territory out of the Mississippi Territory.
Alabama becomes the 22nd state on December 14. Its first constitution protects slavery and blocks the legislature from freeing enslaved people.
On September 27, the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek takes all Choctaw land east of the Mississippi River; most Choctaws are forced to Indian Territory starting in 1831.
After the Treaty of Cusseta (1832) and the Second Creek War, the U.S. forces most Creeks to move west to Indian Territory.
U.S. troops force Cherokees from Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina, and Tennessee; about one-fourth of the Cherokee people die during removal.
On July 8, the Clotilda illegally brings enslaved Africans to Mobile, decades after the U.S. banned the international slave trade. Survivors later found African Town (Africatown) north of Mobile.
Alabama secedes from the Union on January 11 (vote of 61 to 39). Montgomery serves as the first capital of the Confederacy from February to May 1861.
In June, Congress readmits Alabama to the Union under a new constitution. Black men serve in the state legislature.
Democrats regain full control of state government, and Reconstruction ends in Alabama; an 1875 constitution undoes much of the Reconstruction government's work.

trailblazers.name: Oluale Kossola (Cudjo Lewis)
trailblazers.text: Kossola was taken from West Africa and brought to Mobile on the Clotilda in 1860. After freedom, he and his wife Abile bought land and helped build African Town (Africatown) north of Mobile. Writer Zora Neale Hurston filmed him in his later years.

trailblazers.name: James T. Rapier
trailblazers.text: Rapier was elected to the U.S. Congress in 1872, one of three Black Republican congressmen from Alabama during Reconstruction. He supported the Civil Rights Act of 1875 and ran the Montgomery Republican State Sentinel, Alabama's first African American-owned newspaper.

trailblazers.name: Helen Keller
trailblazers.text: Born in Tuscumbia, Keller lost her sight and hearing as a young child. With her teacher Anne Sullivan, who arrived in 1887, she learned to communicate and graduated from Radcliffe College in 1904. She spent her life working for people with disabilities, women's rights, and racial equality.

trailblazers.name: Rosa Parks
trailblazers.text: Born in Tuskegee, Parks was active in the Montgomery NAACP and served as secretary to its president, E.D. Nixon. On December 1, 1955, she was arrested in Montgomery for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger. Her arrest became the rallying point for the Montgomery Bus Boycott, which lasted 381 days; a federal court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional, and the U.S. Supreme Court upheld that ruling on November 13, 1956.

trailblazers.name: Mae Jemison
trailblazers.text: Born in Decatur, Jemison studied chemical engineering at Stanford and medicine at Cornell. In September 1992 she flew on Space Shuttle Endeavour, becoming the first African American woman in space.

trailblazers.name: Lynn McGhee
trailblazers.text: McGhee, a cattleman, ferry operator, and interpreter, fought for more than thirty years to keep his family's land in southwest Alabama after the Creek War. His family's community became the Poarch Band of Creek Indians, which won federal recognition in 1984.

waters: Alabama River (formed by the Coosa and Tallapoosa)
Chattahoochee River (part of the Georgia border)
Lake Guntersville (largest lake, a reservoir of about 69,000 acres)
geography.regions: Alabama has five natural sections: the Highland Rim and Cumberland Plateau in the north, the Tennessee Valley and Ridge and the Piedmont Upland in the northeast, and the wide East Gulf Coastal Plain across the south.

ecosystems.name: Longleaf pine forest
ecosystems.about: Longleaf pine once covered about 90 million acres of North America, but only about 2.7 million acres remain. Lightning fires every few years keep the forest open for gopher tortoises, red-cockaded woodpeckers, and pitcher plants.

ecosystems.name: Mobile-Tensaw River Delta
ecosystems.about: Over 260,000 acres of lakes, streams, swamps, and bayous, nicknamed "America's Amazon." The basin has more tree species than any other region in North America.

ecosystems.name: Gulf Coast and Mobile Bay
ecosystems.about: Bon Secour National Wildlife Refuge on the Gulf Coast has recorded over 370 species of birds.

science.weather: Humid subtropical: hot summers, mild winters, rain in every season. Alabama averages about 20 tornadoes a year, with spring and fall seasons; the April 27, 2011, outbreak sent more than 50 tornadoes across the state. Hurricanes (season May through October) strike the coast about once every 16 years, such as Frederic (1979) and Ivan (2004). Snow is rare.
science.resources: Iron ore, coal, limestone, and dolomite found close together near Birmingham made it an iron and steel center; forests of pine are another major resource.
science.highlight: Basilosaurus cetoides, the state fossil, was an ancient whale that grew 60 to 70 feet long and swam in a shallow sea that covered southern Alabama about 34 to 35 million years ago. Many skeletons have been found in Choctaw and Clarke counties.

g3_ss.title: Alabama's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Montgomery, Huntsville, Mobile, and Birmingham; learn the three branches (Legislature with 35 senators and 105 representatives, governor, Supreme Court with 9 justices) and the 67 counties; read Article I, Section 2 together.

g3_ss.title: Alabama's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Visit Moundville in pictures, compare Muscogee (Creek), Choctaw, and Cherokee ways of life, and meet the Poarch Band of Creek Indians, a nation in Alabama today.

g3_ss.title: Alabama Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Short biographies of Rosa Parks, Helen Keller, Mae Jemison, and Cudjo Lewis, with a 'how they changed Alabama' card for each.

g45_ss.title: Alabama's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Moundville's mound town (c. 1120), Creek towns and the busk, Choctaw and Cherokee homelands; then the Creek War, Horseshoe Bend, and removal in the 1830s told from Indigenous points of view.

g45_ss.title: Spanish, French, and British Alabama
g45_ss.plan: De Soto and Mabila (1540), French Mobile (1702 and 1711), British West Florida (1763), and Gálvez's capture of Mobile (1780); who gained and who lost at each step.

g45_ss.title: Alabama 1817–1877
g45_ss.plan: Territory to statehood (1819), cotton and slavery, the Clotilda and Africatown (1860), secession and Montgomery as Confederate capital (1861), and Reconstruction leaders like James T. Rapier (1868–1874).

g3_sci.title: Longleaf Pine Forests
g3_sci.plan: How fire helps a forest; meet the gopher tortoise and red-cockaded woodpecker; plant life cycle of the grass-stage pine.

g3_sci.title: Tornadoes and Hurricanes
g3_sci.plan: Why Alabama has spring and fall tornado seasons and Gulf hurricanes; build a family safety plan.

g3_sci.title: Alabama's Rivers and Delta
g3_sci.plan: Trace rivers to Mobile Bay and explore the Mobile-Tensaw Delta's swamps and wildlife.

g45_sci.title: Ancient Whales of Alabama
g45_sci.plan: Fossils and rock layers: how Basilosaurus shows a sea once covered southern Alabama 34 to 35 million years ago.

g45_sci.title: Rocks That Built a City
g45_sci.plan: Iron ore, coal, and limestone near Birmingham; how minerals become steel and what mining changes in the land.

g45_sci.title: Biodiversity in America's Amazon
g45_sci.plan: Food webs and wetlands of the Mobile-Tensaw Delta; why wetlands matter during floods and storms.
